analysis.one_liner: Erases fully paid or settled medical bills from consumer credit reports.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 336-82 with bipartisan backing in September 2010, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a medical bill lands in collections and a person later pays it off or settles it, that record can still drag down their credit score for years. The bill would have barred credit reporting agencies from listing medical debt once it had been fully paid or settled, allowing only a 45-day window for the final entry. The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin; the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 72 million working-age adults the bill cited as affected by medical bill problems, especially the 28 million contacted by collection agencies over unpaid medical bills in a single year. People who paid off or settled a medical collection could stop having that old bill suppress their credit score, which affects the interest rates they pay on mortgages, credit cards, and car loans, and can affect apartment applications and some job checks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who paid off medical bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to bar consumer reporting agencies from including information about a fully paid or settled medical debt that had been in collection, once 45 days have passed since payment or settlement.

The bill's findings state that medical bills account for more than half of all non-credit-related collection items reported to credit agencies, and that a paid-off medical collection can significantly damage a consumer's score for years, leading to denied credit or higher interest rates on homes and credit cards.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies would lose a category of data that feeds the credit scores they sell to lenders. Debt collectors would lose a reporting tool, since the threat of a credit ding is part of how unpaid bills get paid. Lenders would see a slightly thinner record of an applicant's past bills.

drawbacks.text: The fix is narrow: it covers only medical debt that has been fully paid or settled. Unpaid medical collections would still appear on credit reports and still damage scores, so most of the medical debt dragging on consumers would remain.
The bill allows a 45-day reporting window after payment or settlement, so a paid medical bill could still briefly appear on a report before it must come off.

Lenders lose some information: excluding paid medical collections means a lender reviewing a report no longer sees that part of an applicant's history, which is the standard objection lenders raise to narrowing credit data.
Credit evaluators themselves acknowledge medical collections are frequently disputed and inconsistently reported, which is exactly why the industry's own practice around this data has been contested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: millions of people who actually paid their medical bills would no longer be penalized for them for years afterward, at little direct cost to anyone but the data companies. The main honest caveat is scope — because it only covers paid or settled debt, it would not help the person still carrying the unpaid medical bill. It is a modest, well-aimed repair, not a comprehensive medical debt fix.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 336-82 on a September 29, 2010 vote, and the Senate sent it to its Banking Committee, which never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced in July 2009 by Rep. Mary Jo Kilroy, the bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee for nearly a year before a markup on July 28, 2010 ordered it reported by voice vote.

The House took it up under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure reserved for non-controversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority; a first attempt on September 28 was postponed after a quorum objection, and the bill passed the next day 336-82, with 249 of 253 voting House Democrats in favor and Republicans split 87-81.

The Senate received the bill on September 29, 2010 and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer reporting agencies and the debt collection industry are better off, because the bill never became law and paid medical bills continued to count against consumers' credit scores. Lenders also keep the fuller data picture.

industries.note: The bill would have forced the bureaus to delete paid or settled medical collections, data that feeds the credit scores they sell to lenders, and the bill's findings note that such entries often generate disputes. Because the bill died, bureaus kept the data and consumers kept the score damage.

A collection item's power to hurt a credit score is part of what makes people pay; the bill would have removed that leverage once a medical bill was settled. The industry's interest in keeping the reporting threat ran against consumers who had already paid.
The bill left providers' ability to collect and to send unpaid bills to agencies untouched, so their billing operations were unaffected; they lose nothing and gain nothing from the reporting change.
Lenders would see a thinner credit file with no paid medical collections, losing some information about applicants while fewer applicants would be unfairly penalized by bills they already paid.
